content: King County, located in Washington State, is home to approximately 8 million residents. The county offers several unique public health services, including King County Medic One, specialized health services for gay and lesbian populations, online restaurant inspection reports, and weekly healthy recipe recommendations. Public Health – Seattle & King County (PHSKC) has earned a growing reputation as the CDC-West due to its internationally recognized expertise in communicable diseases and epidemiology. The history of public health in Seattle dates back to 1877, when the Seattle City Council established the position of Health Officer. This role was created to address public health nuisances and prevent the spread of contagious diseases, particularly smallpox. Between 1877 and 1890, ten different local physicians served as Health Officers. In 1890, under the city’s first home rule charter, the Department of Sanitation was established under the supervision of the Board of Health, which had the authority to appoint a Health Officer. The Board of Health was tasked with overseeing the city’s health and sanitation efforts. In 1891, a Market Inspector was appointed under the Health Officer’s supervision to regulate sanitation in Seattle’s public markets. In 1908, a City Charter amendment dissolved the Board of Health and replaced it with a new Department of Health, which was administered by a Commissioner of Health appointed by the Mayor. For a detailed account of the health and sanitation department’s history from 1877 to 1943, researchers are advised to consult pages 77–107 of the 1939–1943 Annual Report. In 1951, Seattle’s Department of Health merged with the King County Department of Health. Prior to 1981, the City of Seattle managed the department, with funding provided by both the city and county in proportion to their respective populations. A reorganization in 1981 transferred administrative control to King County, while the City of Seattle retained direct policy and funding control over the Seattle Services Division. In July 2006, a tragic incident occurred when a Public Health employee, Maritza Rios-Dowe, was attacked by a mentally disturbed woman who had entered the facility from the street. The attack left Rios-Dowe severely injured and permanently blinded in both eyes. The assailant had a documented history of violent behavior toward strangers and was subsequently found criminally insane. She was committed to a local mental health institution.
